content.p: In the first days of December 2018, an armed group seized a camp of bridge builders in the mountains of Nduga Regency, in Indonesia's Papua province, and marched them away. Indonesian police later said that 19 workers and one soldier had been killed, which Asia Times described as the worst single incident in the province on record. The West Papua National Liberation Army, known as the TPNPB, said it carried out the attacks. It also said the dead were not civilians but soldiers in disguise. The government rejected that.

Almost everything about the event was disputed: the number of dead, the day the shootings happened, who the victims were, and what the security forces did in the villages afterwards. Journalists could not get to Nduga. Human Rights Watch said at the time that no reporters had been able to reach the area since the attacks.

The workers belonged to PT Istaka Karya, a state-owned contractor. They were building a bridge on the Trans Papua Highway, one of President Joko Widodo's flagship projects. The Diplomat put the whole route at some 4,325 kilometres, and the Jakarta Post said the section in question linked Wamena with Mamugu. Asia Times said the dead had been employed on a single bridge among 35 planned along the 270-kilometre Wamena to Kenyam and Mamugu section. HRW's account, quoting Indonesia's public works minister Basuki Hadimuljono, was that the workers came from Istaka Karya and a second state firm, PT Brantas Abipraya, and had been sent from Sulawesi.

The road is welcomed by some and feared by others. Asia Times reported that Papuan leaders worried about migrants, who by its estimate already outnumbered indigenous Papuans by as much as 60 to 40 across the once-roadless territory. The Diplomat noted that the armed independence movement saw the highway as a way for Jakarta to extend its reach into remote interior regions. DW quoted the Papua observer Made Supriatma saying that if asked who would benefit from the infrastructure, Papuans would reply that they did not want it.

Behind this lay a longer quarrel. Papua had declared itself independent under Dutch rule in 1961, and Indonesia took control with a United Nations-backed vote in 1969, which Al Jazeera described as widely seen as a sham and the Diplomat said was a vote of 1,026 tribal leaders. Each year, 1 December is marked by many Papuans as the day the Morning Star flag was first raised beside the Dutch flag. Flying that flag is banned. On 1 December 2018 HRW said more than 500 students were arrested in more than ten Indonesian cities for raising it; the Guardian recorded activists' claims of almost 600 arrests.
content.h2: The camp, the photographs and the march
content.p: A report by a rescue team of church leaders, Nduga government representatives, local legislators and civil-society figures, published by the International Coalition for Papua, gives the most detailed account of the lead-up. It said that in 2017 TPNPB members had agreed with workers that every year they would leave the camp on 24 November, so as not to disturb the 1 December commemorations. In 2018, it said, project management did not let them go before that date, and only a few left, fearing that the fighters would feel provoked by their presence.

According to the same report, on 1 December the project supervisor, Joni Arung, and a colleague attended a church service and the cooking of a pig in Wuridlak village. Egianus Kogoya and his men were there. When Arung took photographs of the fighters, Kogoya was angry. He suspected the man of working with the security services, seized his phone, threatened to kill him if he would not unlock it, and then ordered the arrest of all the workers at the camp. Indonesian police had also initially said the killings were retribution for a worker photographing a flag-raising, as HRW reported, and Asia Times carried the same early account.

What happened next depends on the source. The rescue team said fighters went to the camp on 2 December and took 24 employees, tied their hands and led them to Kabo mountain between Yigi and Mbua districts, where they killed those they suspected of being soldiers. Some workers, it said, were allegedly released because the fighters believed they were civilians.

The Jakarta Post relayed a survivor's account that Indonesian military commanders had passed on. Jimmi Aritonang said an armed group took 25 workers from the camp on Saturday and marched them to the Karunggame river. On Sunday they were moved toward Puncak Kabo hill, ordered to squat in five rows and shot. By his account 14 died on the spot and 11 pretended to be dead. The gunmen found some of them as they tried to escape, killing five, and six got away toward Mbua. The Jakarta Post noted that the national police chief's figure of 19 workers dead seemed to rest on this account. The Diplomat's version, citing an eyewitness, was that 25 were abducted and four escaped by playing dead.
content.h2: The count, and who the dead were
content.p: The numbers moved. Papua police first said they feared 31 workers had been killed. Istaka Karya's president, Sigit Inarto, said only 28 workers had been at the site. The Guardian reported differing counts of 24 to 31 dead in Indonesian media, and the TPNPB put its own figure for the first attack at 24. Police chief Tito Karnavian and the security minister Wiranto then confirmed on 5 December that 20 were dead: 19 workers and one soldier. BenarNews said authorities did not explain the gap. Later press reports used 16, 17 and 19 for the workers. A joint security team found 15 bodies on 5 December, but could not at that stage say if all were Istaka Karya employees. HRW headlined its report with 17 dead. Al Jazeera, a week after the event, spoke of at least 16, and quoted Indonesian authorities saying most of the victims' hands were tied and that some had gunshot, knife or blunt-force wounds. At least four workers were still missing.

The rescue team's own report said that security forces evacuated 17 bodies, all of them Istaka Karya employees, and that its mission on 13 December set out to recover the remains of four more who were still missing.

The soldier's death came in a separate attack. Asia Times said that on 3 December a soldier died when the separatists attacked a nearby security post. The Jakarta Post said the post sheltering survivors was attacked early on Monday with guns, arrows and spears, one soldier killed and another injured. The rescue team report put the attack on the 756 military post in Mbuwa on 3 December at 6 a.m., with an exchange of fire lasting until 6 p.m. Tempo later named the soldier as Handoko.

Who the dead were was the sharpest dispute. TPNPB spokesman Sebby Sambom told BenarNews that "it was a gunfight, not an execution", and that his group had watched the workers for months and knew them to be members of an army combat-engineering unit. He told DW the same and added that the group rejected the infrastructure. Indonesia's public works minister said they were civilian workers and that only the soldiers protecting them were armed. HRW reported that an army colonel said three of the survivors were military engineers. Human rights lawyer Veronica Koman told the Guardian that the information was "messy", and that, according to previous reports, road workers in that area had "always been the military", but that the Guardian could not verify any of it. The Guardian said it could not independently check the accounts.

President Widodo said there was "no room" for such armed groups and ordered the army chief and police chief to pursue and capture all perpetrators. He said the road project would carry on. Defence and security officials rejected negotiation: Wiranto declared "I won't hold talks with criminals". Presidential chief of staff Moeldoko called the killings terrorism by the Free Papua Movement, but also urged police and military to be professional and proportionate and not to take revenge. Construction of the bridges in Nduga was suspended pending a security review, according to a road agency official quoted by BenarNews. The Diplomat reported that the army said it would take over the construction projects.

Ahmad Taufan Damanik, chair of the National Human Rights Commission, Komnas HAM, called the actions "brutal and inhumane" and asked for the suspects to be arrested and the case handled transparently. He also asked the president to guarantee witness protection and the costs of recovery for victims and witnesses. Amnesty International Indonesia's Usman Hamid warned that the attacks must not become a pretext to roll back freedoms. At least 169 soldiers and police had been sent to Nduga by 5 December, according to BenarNews, and HRW said more than 100 officers were evacuating the dead and injured and conducting an operation against the militants.

The armed group refused to back down. On 10 December Sambom read an open letter to Widodo in a YouTube video, demanding another referendum for Papuans. Al Jazeera quoted him saying the TPNPB would not surrender before independence was achieved.

Accounts of what the security forces did after 3 December came from villagers and church workers, and the government disputed them. The rescue team report said that on 4 December ground troops closed in from Jayawijaya and four military helicopters from Timika were sent to Kenyam. Eyewitnesses claimed one helicopter dropped seven explosives and the others fired heavy machine guns at several villages. The team said it was unclear what explosives were used. The operation, it said, went on until 10 December.

Al Jazeera reported that the Free Papua Movement accused the military of killing civilians in operations that it said included bombings. Wiranto rejected that accusation, though he said soldiers had used grenades in clashes.

When the rescue team reached villages in Mbuwa district from 13 December, it said it found two 18-year-old men dead, Nison Umangge and Mianus Elokbere, and returned them to their families. Both, the villagers said, were shot as they fled into the forest when helicopters attacked on 4 December. Another young man, Mentus Nimiangge, aged 21, was met by the team with a bullet wound near the neck and died on 15 December, according to the report, after security forces were not able to evacuate him by helicopter. Villagers also alleged that Rabu Gwijangge was shot dead on 5 December in Wuridlak village after soldiers got out of a helicopter, and that military officers ordered residents not to leave their houses between 5 and 12 December. These are allegations in a report by a civil-society team. The team's missions to find the missing workers' bodies were broken off on 14 and 15 December after security forces followed it toward Kabo mountain.

The fighting emptied villages. The 2019 US State Department report on human rights in Indonesia said the clashes between the Free Papua Movement and security forces displaced thousands of civilians and caused serious humanitarian concern, and that little information was available on the numbers of civilians, security personnel and separatists killed or injured. In August 2019 the Jakarta Post reported that volunteers in the Nduga Solidarity Civil Society Coalition counted 182 civilians who had died while sheltering after fleeing, between December and July, of hunger and illness. An earlier count of 139 had been rejected by the government as a hoax. The government's own figure was 53. The coalition said tens of thousands had fled to forests and neighbouring regencies. A military spokesman said he had no update on the toll and that data and perceptions of the causes might differ.

Violence did not stop in Nduga. In January 2019 the Free Papua Movement said it backed a declaration of war by its armed wing, according to Radio New Zealand as cited by Tempo. Tempo reported that on 2 February 2019 a 25-year-old kiosk keeper, Sugeng Efendi, was shot dead in Jayawijaya, and the Papua police chief warned that the armed groups would remain a threat in the central mountains.

No source opened here reports a trial of anyone for the December killings. Egianus Kogoya was named by the TPNPB itself and by Indonesian authorities as the commander behind the attack; the Papuan group's spokesman Sebby Sambom said operations commander Pemne Kogeya was also involved. A court has not established their roles in anything the sources describe.
